{{Short description|Rhetorical cliché phrase}}
{{good article}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=January 2022}}
[[File:Think of the children collage.jpg|thumb|alt=Typed statements with different sizes and fonts on a white background. The statements all include the phrase "think of the children" |Five uses of "think of the children" before the [[United States Congress]]]]
"'''Think of the children'''" (also "'''What about the children?'''") is a [[cliché]] that evolved into a [[rhetoric]]al tactic. In the literal sense, it refers to [[children's rights]] (as in discussions of [[child labor]]). In debate, it is a [[Appeal to pity|plea for pity]] that is used as an [[appeal to emotion]], and therefore may become a [[formal fallacy|logical fallacy]].

==History==
''Art, Argument, and Advocacy'' (2002) argued that the appeal substitutes [[emotion]] for [[reason]] in debate.<ref name="meany" /> [[Ethics|Ethicist]] Jack Marshall wrote in 2005 that the phrase's popularity stems from its capacity to stunt [[rationality]], particularly discourse on [[moral]]s.<ref name="jackmarshall" /> "Think of the children" has been invoked by [[censorship]] proponents to shield children from perceived danger.<ref name="beattie2009" /><ref name="keenangt4" /> ''Community, Space and Online Censorship'' (2009) argued that classifying children in an [[infantile]] manner, as innocents in need of protection, is a form of obsession over the concept of purity.<ref name="beattie2009" /> A 2011 article in the ''Journal for Cultural Research'' observed that the phrase grew out of a [[moral panic]].<ref name="coleman2011" />

It was an exhortation in the 1964 [[Walt Disney Productions|Disney]] film ''[[Mary Poppins (film)|Mary Poppins]]'', when the character of Mrs. Banks pleaded with her departing [[nanny]] not to quit and to "think of the children!"<ref name="kathrynlaity" /> The phrase was popularized as a [[satire|satiric]] reference on the animated television program ''[[The Simpsons]]'' in 1996,<ref name="cohen1996" /><ref name="cohen2005" /> when character [[Helen Lovejoy]] pleaded variations of "Will someone please think of the children?"<ref name="tenbrink2012" /><ref name="shotwell2012" /><ref name="keenanin2" /> multiple times during a contentious debate by citizens of the fictional town of [[Springfield (The Simpsons)|Springfield]].<ref name="tenbrink2012" /><ref name="patrick2000" /><ref name="kitrosser2011" />

In the 2012 ''[[Georgia State University Law Review]]'', Charles J. Ten Brink called Lovejoy's use of "Think of the children" a successful [[parody]].<ref name="tenbrink2012" /> The appeal's subsequent use in society was often the subject of mockery.<ref name="keenangt4" /> After its popularization on ''The Simpsons'', an appeal to the welfare of children has been called "Lovejoy's Law",<ref name="keenanin2" /> the "Lovejoy argument", the "Mrs. Lovejoy fallacy",<ref>{{cite tweet |user=linkskywalker |number=192789880168914944 |title=The Appeal to Reproduction can alternatively be dubbed "the Mrs. Lovejoy Fallacy" if you are so inclined. |date=18 April 2012}}</ref> the "Helen Lovejoy defence", "Helen Lovejoy syndrome",<ref name="hunt2014" /> the "Lovejoy Trap",<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hamad |first1=Ruby |title=White tears brown scars : how white feminism betrays women of color |date=2020 |location=New York |isbn=9781948226745 |language=en}}</ref> and "think-of-the-children-ism".<ref name="penny2011" /><ref name="bruenig" />

In 2018, author [[Nassim Nicholas Taleb]] coined the term 'pedophrasty' for an argument "involving children to prop up a rationalization ... Often done with the aid of pictures".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Taleb |first=Nassim Nicholas |date=2019-06-16 |title=Pedophrasty, Bigoteering, and Other Modern Scams |url=https://medium.com/incerto/pedophrasty-bigoteering-and-other-modern-scams-c84bd70a29e8 |access-date=2023-11-07 |website=INCERTO |language=en}}</ref>

==Child advocacy==

{{quote box |width=25em | bgcolor=#c6dbf7 |align=right |salign=right|quote=Think of the children&nbsp;... freed of the crushing burden of dangerous and demeaning work.|source=[[Bill Clinton]]<ref name="clinton1999" />}}

"Think of the children" has been used in its literal sense to advocate for the rights of children.<ref name="nationalchild" /><ref name="boyce2003" /><ref name="perry2010" /> Early usage during the 20th century included writings in 1914 by the [[National Child Labor Committee]] criticizing [[child labor]] standards in the United States.<ref name="nationalchild">National Child Labor Committee 1914, pp. 39, 73.</ref> U.S. President [[Bill Clinton]] used the phrase in a 1999 speech to the [[International Labour Organization]],<ref name="clinton1999" /> asking his audience to imagine a significant reduction in child labor: "Think of the children&nbsp;... freed of the crushing burden of dangerous and demeaning work, given back those irreplaceable hours of childhood for learning and playing and living."<ref name="clinton1999">Clinton 1999</ref>

The phrase's literal use extends into the 21st century, with Sara Boyce of the Children's Law Centre in [[Northern Ireland]] drawing on it to advocate for the legal rights of the region's children.<ref name="boyce2003">Boyce 2003</ref> The 2008 book ''Child Labour in a Globalized World'' used the phrase to call attention to the role of [[debt bondage]] in child labor.<ref name="nesi2008">Nesi 2008, p. 7.</ref> Sara Dillon of [[Suffolk University Law School]] used the phrase "What about the children" in her 2009 book, ''International Children's Rights'', to focus on child-labor program conditions.<ref name="dillon2009">Dillon 2009, p. 117.</ref> [[Benjamin Powell]] used the phrase differently in his book, ''Out of Poverty: Sweatshops in the Global Economy'', writing that in the absence of child labor, some youth faced [[starvation]].<ref name="powell2014">Powell 2014, p. 5.</ref> In a 2010 book on [[human rights]], ''Children's Rights and Human Development'', child [[psychiatrist]] [[Bruce D. Perry]] used the phrase "think of the children" to urge clinicians to incorporate a process sensitive to developmental stages when counseling youth.<ref name="perry2010">Perry 2010, p. 498.</ref>

==Debate tactic==

===Logical fallacy===
In their 2002 book, ''Art, Argument, and Advocacy: Mastering Parliamentary Debate'', John Meany and Kate Shuster called the use of the phrase "Think of the children" in debate a type of [[formal fallacy|logical fallacy]] and an [[appeal to emotion]].<ref name="meany" /> According to the authors, a debater may use the phrase to [[emotion]]ally sway members of the audience and avoid [[logic]]al discussion.<ref name="meany" /> They provide an example: "I know this national missile defense plan has its detractors, but won't someone ''please'' think of the children?"<ref name="meany">Meany 2002, p. 65.</ref> Their assessment was echoed by Margie Borschke in an article for the journal ''Media International Australia incorporating Culture and Policy'', with Borschke calling its use a [[rhetoric]]al tactic.<ref name="borschke2011">Borschke 2011, p. 17.</ref>

[[Ethicist]] Jack Marshall described "Think of the children!" as a tactic used in an attempt to end discussion by invoking an unanswerable argument.<ref name="jackmarshall">Marshall 2005</ref> According to Marshall, the strategy succeeds in preventing rational debate.<ref name="jackmarshall" /> He called its use an [[Ethics|unethical]] manner of obfuscating debate, misdirecting [[empathy]] towards an object which may not have been the focus of the original argument.<ref name="jackmarshall" /> Marshall wrote that although the phrase's use may have a positive intention, it evokes [[irrationality]] when repeatedly used by both sides of a debate.<ref name="jackmarshall" /> He concluded that the phrase can transform the observance of regulations into an ethical quandary, cautioning society to avoid using "Think of the children!" as a final argument.<ref name="jackmarshall" />

In his 2015 syndicated article "Think Of The Children", [[Michael Reagan]] criticized the phrase's use by politicians.<ref name="michaelreagan2015">Reagan 2015</ref> According to Reagan, politicians needed to stop using children as tools when arguing for favored governmental programs.<ref name="michaelreagan2015" /> He called the tactic an illogical argument, an act of desperation by those who felt they had a weaker case with reason-based arguments.<ref name="michaelreagan2015" /> Noting that it has been used by [[Democratic party (United States)|Democrats]] and [[Republican party (United States)|Republicans]] alike in the United States,<ref name="michaelreagan2015" /> Reagan called the tactic "obvious political BS".<ref name="michaelreagan2015" />

===Moral panic===
[[File:2015 Think of the Children by Mia Love.ogv|thumb|alt=Link to a video of Congresswoman Mia Love|The phrase, used by Congresswoman [[Mia Love]]]]

The ''Journal for Cultural Research'' published an article in 2010 by Debra Ferreday,<ref name="ferreday2010">Ferreday 2010, pp. 409–429.</ref> which was republished in the 2011 book ''Hope and Feminist Theory''.<ref name="coleman2011">Coleman 2011, p. 99.</ref> According to Ferreday, media use of "Won't someone think of the children!" had become common in a climate of [[moral panic]].<ref name="coleman2011" /> She suggested that the phrase was becoming so common that it could become another [[Godwin's law]].<ref name="coleman2011" />

In a 2011 article for the journal ''Post Script'', Andrew Scahill wrote about the power of children in rhetoric to create an untenable stance for an opposing viewpoint.<ref name="scahill2011" /> According to Scahill, an individual arguing "for the children" makes it extremely difficult for an opponent to hold a "not for the children" position.<ref name="scahill2011">Scahill 2011, pp.&nbsp;69–81.</ref> [[Cassandra Wilkinson]] discussed the impact of "think of the children" rhetoric in a 2011 article for ''[[IPA Review]]''.<ref name="berg2011">Berg 2011</ref> Wilkinson cited research by ''No Fear: Growing Up in a Risk-Averse Society'' author Tim Gill that hypersensitivity in defending children from potential harm has the adverse effect of contributing to the inability of youth to own their choices and react to dangerous situations.<ref name="wilkinson2011">Wilkinson 2011</ref> In the ''[[New Statesman]]'', [[Laurie Penny]] characterized the tactic as a political belief system and called it "think-of-the-children-ism".<ref name="penny2011">{{Cite web |last=Penny| first=Laurie |date=2011-01-17 |title=this divorce tax is emotional terrorism |url=https://www.newstatesman.com/politics/2011/01/women-children-tax-welfare |website=New Statesman |language=en-GB}}</ref>

[[Elizabeth Bruenig]] wrote in a 2014 article for ''[[First Things]]'' that [[moralizing]] with the phrase was commonly seen in discussions of [[sexuality]],<ref name="bruenig">Bruenig 2014</ref> attributing this to society's increasing perception of morality as a [[femininity|feminine]] domain.<ref name="bruenig" /> Bruenig also cited the labeling of [[NBC]]'s refusal to broadcast a movie trailer about [[abortion]] as "think-of-the-children-ism".<ref name="bruenig" /> The argument is also routinely used in discussions around [[Recreational drug use|drug use]] and [[drug policy]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bright |first=Stephen |date=2015-11-10 |title=Won't somebody think of the children? Five reasons why drug panics are counterproductive |url=https://theconversation.com/wont-somebody-think-of-the-children-five-reasons-why-drug-panics-are-counterproductive-50078 |access-date=2024-08-23 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

===<span class="anchor" id="Censorship tool"></span>Censorship===
Scott Beattie wrote in his 2009 book, ''Community, Space and Online Censorship'', that the question "Will no one think of the children?" was often raised by individuals advocating [[censorship]] out of a concern that youth might view material deemed inappropriate.<ref name="beattie2009">Beattie 2009, pp. 165–167.</ref> According to Beattie, youngsters were cast as potential casualties of [[Online child abuse|online sexual predators]] to increase regulation of the [[Internet]]; characterizing children as [[infantilization|infantile]] evoked a concept of innocence which was a form of obsession over the concept of purity.<ref name="beattie2009" />

For ''[[Make (magazine)|Make]]'' magazine, [[Cory Doctorow]] wrote in a 2011 article that "Won't someone think of the children?!" was used by irrational individuals to support arguments about the dangers to youth of the "[[Four Horsemen of the Infocalypse]]": "[[copyright infringement|pirates]]", [[terrorist]]s, [[organized crime]], and [[child pornography|child pornographers]].<ref name="doctorow2011">Doctorow 2011, p. 31.</ref> According to Doctorow, the phrase was used to stifle discussion of underlying issues and halt [[rational analysis]].<ref name="doctorow2011" /> He observed its frequent use when society was determining an appropriate approach to the [[legal aspects of computing]].<ref name="doctorow2011" />

In his 2013 book, ''Fervid Filmmaking'', Mike Watt discussed the history of [[censorship]] relative to the [[United Kingdom]]'s [[Obscene Publications Act 1959]] and noted that films banned during that period became known as "[[Video nasty|video nasties]]".<ref name="watt2013" /> Watt called a current interpretation of such censorship the "Think of the Children" characterization.<ref name="watt2013">Watt 2013, p. 233.</ref> Brian M. Reed wrote in his book, ''Nobody's Business'' (also published that year), that the phrase was devoid of substance and could be replaced for comic effect with "How many kittens must die?"<ref name="reed2013">Reed 2013, p. 110.</ref>

For ''[[Reason (magazine)|Reason]]'' in 2015, journalist [[Brendan O'Neill (journalist)|Brendan O'Neill]] wrote that [[Marjorie Heins]]' ''[[Not in Front of the Children: Indecency, Censorship, and the Innocence of Youth]]'' cited the centuries-long use by governments of the prevention of "harm to minors" as an excuse to increase censorship and control.<ref name="brendanoneill">O'Neill 2015</ref> According to O'Neill, the use of "Won't somebody please think of the children?" in contemporary culture had greatly increased and was a means of exerting [[moral authority]] with [[emotional blackmail]].<ref name="brendanoneill" />

==Popularization==

===Film and television===
According to Kathryn Laity, early use of the phrase may have stemmed from its appearance in the 1964 [[Walt Disney Pictures]] film ''[[Mary Poppins (film)|Mary Poppins]]''.<ref name="kathrynlaity">Laity 2013, pp.&nbsp;118–119, 128.</ref> In an opening scene, the character of Mrs. Banks pleads with her nanny not to quit by begging her to "think of the children!".<ref name="kathrynlaity" /> Laity wrote that the popular use of the phrase evokes strong feelings in those who object to a [[nanny state]],<ref name="kathrynlaity" /> pointing out the conflict in the United States between the country's conservatism (derived from the [[Puritans]]) and its desire to use [[sex in advertising]].<ref name="kathrynlaity" />

Before the phrase's exposure in ''The Simpsons'', most Americans first became accustomed to it during the 1980s in a charity commercial with [[Sally Struthers]] for [[Christian Children's Fund]]. At the end of the commercial Struthers pleaded with the viewers, "Won't somebody please think of the children?" It was also used in [[John Huston]]'s 1982 film ''[[Annie (1982 film)|Annie]]'', spoken by [[Eleanor Roosevelt]] as Annie sings "[[Tomorrow (song from Annie)|Tomorrow]]" to [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] at the White House in order to get [[Oliver Warbucks]]' begrudging support for [[New Deal]] policies he opposes.

"Think of the children" was popularized largely by character [[Helen Lovejoy]], wife of [[Reverend Lovejoy]], on the television program ''[[The Simpsons]]''.<ref name="tenbrink2012">Ten Brink 2012, p. 789.</ref><ref name="shotwell2012">Shotwell 2012, p. 141.</ref><ref name="keenanin2">Keenan (April 26, 2014), p. IN2.</ref> Lovejoy (who first appeared in 1990)<ref name="groening1997">Groening 1997, p. 25.</ref><ref name="martyn2000">Martyn 2000</ref> repeatedly exclaimed, "Think of the children!" in several episodes of the series.<ref name="keenanin2" /><ref name="sagers2009">Sagers 2009</ref><ref name="televisionweek2008">TelevisionWeek 2008, p. 4.</ref> She first used the phrase in the episode "[[Much Apu About Nothing]]" by [[David X. Cohen]], which aired in 1996, imploring the city mayor to keep bears from crossing the [[wildland–urban interface]].<ref name="cohen1996">Cohen 1996</ref><ref name="cohen2005">Cohen 2005</ref><ref name="chappell2014">Chappell 2014</ref> Lovejoy's exhortation became increasingly overwrought with each subsequent use.<ref name="chappell2014" />

''The Simpsons'' writer [[Bill Oakley]] said in the 2005 [[DVD commentary]] on the episode that the motivation for the phrase on the show was to emphasize how "think of the children" was used in debate; irrelevant, it sidetracked discussion from the original issues.<ref name="cohen2005" /> Lovejoy used variations of the phrase, including "Oh, won't somebody please think of the children"<ref name="cohen1996"/><ref name="patrick2000">Patrick 2000, p. B5.</ref> and "What about the children",<ref name="tenbrink2012" /><ref name="mclennan2009">McLennan 2009, p. A15.</ref> shrieking it most often when residents of the [[List of fictional towns in animation|fictional town]] of [[Springfield (The Simpsons)|Springfield]] debated a contentious problem or argued about [[politics]]<ref name="patrick2000" /><ref name="kitrosser2011">Kitrosser 2011, p. 2395.</ref> and logic failed.<ref name="hunt2014">Hunt 2014, p. 27.</ref> Lovejoy's comic use of the phrase on ''The Simpsons''<ref name="patrick2000" /> [[satire|satirized]] its use in public discourse.<ref name="keenanin2" />

===Lovejoy's Law===
[[File:Think of the children.webm|thumb|alt=Link to clip of Helen Lovejoy, wringing her hands as other characters ignore her or look annoyed|''The Simpsons'' character Helen Lovejoy delivering her signature line, "Ohhh, won't somebody please think of the children!"]]
After the popularization of the phrase on ''The Simpsons'', its use in society was often ridiculed, and came to be referred to as "Lovejoy's Law" in internet culture as early as 2006, probably independently coined several times.<ref name="keenangt4">Keenan (October 1, 2014), p. GT4.</ref> In the ''[[Toronto Star]]'', journalist Edward Keenan defined "Lovejoy's Law" as a warning that the phrase is a probable diversion from a weak logical stance, writing that true empathy toward children involved rational argument rather than manipulation.<ref name="keenanin2" /> In an article for [[Ireland]]'s ''[[Sunday Independent (Ireland)|Sunday Independent]]'', Carol Hunt called the use of the phrase in political debate the "Helen Lovejoy defence" and wrote that it is also known as the "Helen Lovejoy syndrome". According to Hunt, it is often invoked in reference to [[hypothetical]] children rather than real children affected by a problem.<ref name="hunt2014" />

In a ''[[Georgia State University Law Review]]'' article, [[Michigan State University College of Law]] professor Charles J. Ten Brink wrote that Helen Lovejoy's signature phrase was an adept and effective [[parody]].<ref name="tenbrink2012" /> According to ''[[The Canberra Times]]'', the phrase's 2009 use to support [[Internet censorship]] by the [[Department of Communications (Australia)|Department of Communications]] of the [[government of Australia]] was evocative of Helen Lovejoy.<ref name="mclennan2009" />

In his book, ''The Myth of Evil'', Phillip A. Cole wrote that Helen Lovejoy's plea assumed that children were pure, unadulterated potential casualties who required constant defense from danger.<ref name="cole2006">Cole 2006, p. 122.</ref> Cole contrasted this notion with character [[Bart Simpson]], who prefers creating disorder to conformity and adherence to regulations.<ref name="cole2006" /> According to Cole, this exemplifies the dual perception of children by society: guileless potential prey and malevolent entities to be distrusted.<ref name="cole2006" /> Cole wrote that throughout history, the child has represented humanity's savage past and its optimistic future.<ref name="cole2006" /> Jo Johnson contributed a chapter, "Won't Somebody Think of the Children?", to the book ''Mediating Moms'', in which she analyzed the phrase's use in animated media (including ''The Simpsons'').<ref name="jojohnson">Johnson 2012, pp.&nbsp;65–66.</ref> According to Johnson, the phrase was a key example of popular cultural depictions of mothers as neurotic and filled with anxiety about moral values.<ref name="jojohnson" />
